findings.title: Hung/dead spawn processes are never killed because isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) is False for SpawnProcess
findings.body: `_ensure_processes_alive` now only calls `process.kill()` when `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`. Processes are created via `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, which yields `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess`. `SpawnProcess` and `multiprocessing.Process` (`multiprocessing.context.Process`) are sibling subclasses of `BaseProcess`, so the isinstance check is False and `kill()` is skipped. The previous code called `self.process.kill()` unconditionally. Consequence: when a flusher process hangs (cause="hang"), it is left running and a second process is spawned for the same shards, so two processes flush the same Redis shards concurrently and leak until the consumer dies. The same wrong check in `join()` (line 346) means `terminate()` is also never called on real processes. Use `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess)` or check `not isinstance(process, threading.Thread)`.

findings.title: join() stops terminating remaining processes once the deadline passes
findings.body: In `join()`, when `remaining_time <= 0` the loop `break`s before reaching `process.terminate()` for the current and all following processes. Processes that haven't exited by the deadline are thus never terminated (intent of the original code was to terminate after waiting). The `break` should instead skip the wait but still terminate each process.

findings.title: _create_process_for_shard is dead code
findings.body: `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` is never called anywhere; `_ensure_processes_alive` calls `_create_process_for_shards` directly. It also would create a duplicate process without killing the old one. Remove it to avoid confusion.

findings.title: Inconsistent metric tag key ('shards' vs 'shard') and high-cardinality comma-joined tag
findings.body: `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` use tag key `shard` while `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` uses `shards`, making the metrics impossible to correlate by the same tag. Additionally the value is a comma-joined list of all shards in the process (e.g. "0,4,8,12"), whose cardinality depends on partition assignment and process count and will fragment dashboards. Use a consistent key and consider tagging with the process index instead.

findings.title: time.sleep(0.1) in test is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched
findings.body: The test monkeypatches `time.sleep` to `lambda _: None` at the top, then calls `time.sleep(0.1)` with the comment "Give flusher threads time to process after drift change". Since `time.sleep` resolves to the patched attribute, this sleep does nothing, so the comment is misleading and the test only works because `step.join()` waits for the flusher thread. Either remove the sleep or capture the original `sleep` before patching (as `test_flusher.py` does via `from time import sleep`).

findings.title: No test exercises end-to-end flushing with multiple flusher processes/shards
findings.body: `test_flusher_processes_limit` only asserts structural properties (process count and shard assignment) and never submits spans or checks that segments from shards handled by different processes are actually flushed and produced. The multi-process restart path in `_ensure_processes_alive` (per-process healthy_since/restart counters, re-creating a `SpansBuffer` for the shard subset) is also untested. Given this PR changes the core flushing topology, an end-to-end test with >1 process that verifies all shards' segments are produced would catch regressions such as the kill/isinstance bug.

findings.title: Docstring claims one process per shard but default is a single process
findings.body: The class docstring says "Creates one process per shard for parallel processing", but the CLI option `--flusher-processes` defaults to 1 and `num_processes = min(max_processes, len(shards))`, so by default all shards share one process and in general shards are round-robined across at most `max_processes` processes. The docstring should describe the actual behaviour.
